section_title: Can those left in the ruins claim Abraham’s promise while rejecting God’s ways?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 23 Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, 24 “Son of man, those living in the ruins in the land of Israel are saying, ‘Abraham was only one man, yet he possessed the land. But we are many; surely the land has been given to us as a possession.’ 25 Therefore tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘You eat meat with the blood in it, lift up your eyes to your idols, and shed blood. Should you then possess the land? 26 You have relied on your swords, you have committed detestable acts, and each of you has defiled his neighbor’s wife. Should you then possess the land?’

27 Tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘As surely as I live, those in the ruins will fall by the sword, those in the open field I will give to be devoured by wild animals, and those in the strongholds and caves will die by plague. 28 I will make the land a desolate waste, and the pride of her strength will come to an end. The mountains of Israel will become desolate, so that no one will pass through. 29 Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have made the land a desolate waste because of all the abominations they have committed.’

context_lines: Those living among the ruins reason that Abraham was only one man, yet possessed the land. Since they are many, they conclude that it must surely belong to them.

The Lord answers by naming their conduct: eating meat with blood, idolatry, bloodshed, reliance on the sword, detestable practices and adultery. He repeats the question of whether people living this way should possess the land.
The announcement reaches the ruins, fields, strongholds and caves. The Lord will judge the abominations behind their false confidence and bring the land’s proud strength to an end.

The accusation addresses their claim and their behavior. [Jeremiah 39:9–10](https://biblehub.com/bsb/jeremiah/39.htm) also records that Babylon deliberately left some poor people with vineyards and fields; remaining in the land did not by itself explain someone’s faithfulness or wrongdoing.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/33.htm) understands the claim as presumption: people lay claim to blessings while their conduct contradicts the relationship they claim. [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/33.htm) explains their reasoning through descent from Abraham and their presence in the land.

[Cambridge](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/ezekiel/33.htm) sees confidence in the promises without a true knowledge of the Lord whose promises they are. The challenge is not whether Abraham matters, but whether appealing to him can excuse continuing violence and unfaithfulness.
